<!-- slide 45 -->
# Circular Genome Plots {.divider}

[pyCirclize · Circos-style]{.eyebrow}


<!-- slide 46 -->
## Why Circular? {.smaller}

[pyCirclize · theory]{.eyebrow}

### When the x-axis bends back on itself

Most genome views are linear: position on the x-axis, value on the y. That works for one chromosome at a time, and Manhattan plots cheat by laying 22 of them end-to-end. But the moment the *relationships between* chromosomes are the story — a translocation that moves a block from chr3 to chr14, a regulator on chr1 that drives expression on chr19, a Hi-C contact map — a line breaks.

Bend the axis into a circle and three things change:

- Every chromosome becomes the **same visual length** to the eye, regardless of bp.
- You can draw a **chord** between any two points without crossing the figure.
- You can stack many **concentric tracks** (expression, methylation, density) without a vertical spaghetti of axes.

The trade-off: less detail *within* each chromosome (it's a curved sliver), more visibility *across* them. Reach for circular when the answer is in the connections, not the local peaks.


<!-- slide 47 -->
## Anatomy of a Circos Figure {.smaller}

[pyCirclize · theory]{.eyebrow}

### Sectors, tracks, links — the three primitives

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
A circular plot has three building blocks:

- **Sectors** — wedges of the ring, one per chromosome (or contig, or sample). The gap between them is a visual breath.
- **Tracks** — concentric bands at radii `(inner_r, outer_r)`. Each track holds one data layer: scatter, line, bar, heatmap.
- **Links** — chords drawn through the centre, joining two genomic intervals on possibly different sectors.

Build a Circos by declaring the sectors first (`{name: length}`), then adding tracks to each sector and links between them.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6

# CREATE — pure-matplotlib cartoon, no pyCirclize, so the labels stay legible
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6), subplot_kw=dict(aspect="equal"))    # CREATE

# draw four sectors as wedges separated by small gaps
sector_specs = [(0, 80, "chr1", BLUE), (95, 175, "chr2", GREEN),
                (190, 270, "chr3", AMBER), (285, 355, "chr4", PURPLE)]
for theta1, theta2, name, colour in sector_specs:
    # outer track band (90->100) — the "axis" ring                       # CALL
    ax.add_patch(mpatches.Wedge((0, 0), 1.00, theta1, theta2, width=0.10,
                                facecolor=colour, edgecolor=INK, lw=0.5, alpha=0.9))
    # inner data track band (70->88)
    ax.add_patch(mpatches.Wedge((0, 0), 0.88, theta1, theta2, width=0.18,
                                facecolor=CREAM, edgecolor=LINE, lw=0.5))
    # sector label, placed just outside the outer ring
    mid = np.deg2rad((theta1 + theta2) / 2)
    ax.text(1.12 * np.cos(mid), 1.12 * np.sin(mid), name,
            ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11, color=INK, fontweight="bold")

# a single chord (link) — quadratic Bezier through the origin
from matplotlib.patches import FancyArrowPatch
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((0.70 * np.cos(np.deg2rad(40)),  0.70 * np.sin(np.deg2rad(40))),
                             (0.70 * np.cos(np.deg2rad(220)), 0.70 * np.sin(np.deg2rad(220))),
                             connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.25",
                             arrowstyle="-", color=RED, lw=1.4, alpha=0.7))

# annotation arrows / labels                                              # CALL
ax.annotate("sector",          xy=(0.98, 0.55), xytext=(1.45, 0.95),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=MUTED, lw=0.6), fontsize=10, color=MUTED)
ax.annotate("track\n(inner_r, outer_r)", xy=(0.78, -0.40), xytext=(1.30, -0.85),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=MUTED, lw=0.6), fontsize=10, color=MUTED)
ax.annotate("link (chord)",    xy=(0.10, 0.05), xytext=(0.55, -1.35),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=RED,   lw=0.6), fontsize=10, color=RED)
ax.annotate("gap",             xy=(0.95 * np.cos(np.deg2rad(87)),  0.95 * np.sin(np.deg2rad(87))),
            xytext=(-0.10, 1.55),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=MUTED, lw=0.6), fontsize=10, color=MUTED)

ax.set_xlim(-1.7, 1.7); ax.set_ylim(-1.7, 1.7)
ax.axis("off")
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

## Circos · The Data {.smaller}

[pyCirclize · data peek]{.eyebrow}

### Same GWAS table, this time on a ring

`load_gwas("height")` is the table we already met for the Manhattan: one row per SNP, four columns. To draw it circular, we need one extra dictionary — the **length of each chromosome** — which is just `max(pos)` per `chrom`. That dictionary defines the sectors.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column

gwas = load_gwas("height")                # chrom, pos, pval, snp
gwas.head(5)
```

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column

# per-chromosome length = max position on that chromosome
chrom_len = gwas.groupby("chrom")["pos"].max().to_dict()
{k: chrom_len[k] for k in list(chrom_len)[:4]}     # peek at first four
```


<!-- slide 49 -->
## Circos · Step 1 — Just the Sectors {.smaller}

[pyCirclize · build]{.eyebrow}

### 1 · The empty ring

Before any data, build the layout. The `sectors` dict maps chromosome name to length in bp; pyCirclize converts that into proportionally-sized wedges. We give each sector a label and draw — at this point the figure is a labelled empty ring, the canvas every other layer will rest on.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1|3-4|6-8|10-14"}
from pycirclize import Circos                     # the main class

gwas = load_gwas("height")                        # same table as Manhattan
chrom_len = gwas.groupby("chrom")["pos"].max().to_dict()

# sectors: {name: length_in_bp} — order = clockwise order on the ring
sectors = {f"chr{c}": chrom_len[c] for c in sorted(chrom_len)}

circos = Circos(sectors, space=2)                 # CREATE: 2deg gap between sectors

for sector in circos.sectors:
    name = sector.name                                 # pyCirclize: list of Sector(name=...)       # one label per chromosome
    sector.text(name, r=108, size=8, color=INK)   # r = radius (axis is 0-100)

fig = circos.plotfig(figsize=(6.5, 6.5))          # CALL: returns matplotlib Figure
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 6.5

    from pycirclize import Circos
except ImportError as e:
    raise ImportError(
        "pyCirclize is required for this slide. Install with: pip install pycirclize"
    ) from e

for sector in circos.sectors:
    name = sector.name                                 # pyCirclize: list of Sector(name=...)
    sector.text(name, r=108, size=8, color=INK)

fig = circos.plotfig(figsize=(6.5, 6.5))
plt.show()
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 50 -->
## Circos · Step 2 — Axis & Ticks {.smaller}

[pyCirclize · build]{.eyebrow}

### 2 · Give each sector a measuring stick

A ring with no marks is pretty but useless — we can't read positions. `sector.axis()` paints the outer boundary; `sector.xticks_by_interval(...)` drops tick marks at fixed bp intervals so the eye has anchors.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="10-15"}
from pycirclize import Circos

gwas = load_gwas("height")
chrom_len = gwas.groupby("chrom")["pos"].max().to_dict()
sectors = {f"chr{c}": chrom_len[c] for c in sorted(chrom_len)}

circos = Circos(sectors, space=2)                          # CREATE

for sector in circos.sectors:
    name = sector.name                                 # pyCirclize: list of Sector(name=...)
    sector.text(name, r=108, size=8, color=INK)
    # outer axis ring with line styling
    sector.axis(fc=CREAM, ec=INK, lw=0.6)
    # ticks live on a Track, not on the Sector itself — make a thin rim track at
    # the outer edge so the labels orbit the ring without overlapping data.
    rim = sector.add_track((96, 100))
    rim.xticks_by_interval(100_000_000,                                  # every 100 Mb
                           label_size=6, label_orientation="vertical",
                           label_formatter=lambda v: f"{v/1e6:.0f}M")    # bp -> Mb

fig = circos.plotfig(figsize=(6.5, 6.5))                   # CALL
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}

#| fig-width: 6.5

plt.show()
```

<!-- slide 51 -->
## Circos · Step 3 — Manhattan-on-a-Ring {.smaller}

[pyCirclize · build]{.eyebrow}

### 3 · Skyscrapers, pointing outward

Add a scatter **track** at radii `(60, 90)` — a band between 60% and 90% of the ring. For each sector, pull just that chromosome's SNPs out of the GWAS frame and scatter `pos` against `-log10(p)`. Significance now points *outward*: the higher the dot, the closer to the sky.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="11-21"}
from pycirclize import Circos

gwas = load_gwas("height").copy()
gwas["nlog10p"] = -np.log10(gwas["pval"])               # significance axis
chrom_len = gwas.groupby("chrom")["pos"].max().to_dict()
sectors = {f"chr{c}": chrom_len[c] for c in sorted(chrom_len)}

circos = Circos(sectors, space=2)                       # CREATE

for sector in circos.sectors:
    name = sector.name                                 # pyCirclize: list of Sector(name=...)
    sector.text(name, r=108, size=8, color=INK)
    sector.axis(fc=CREAM, ec=INK, lw=0.6)

    # add a track at radii 60-90 (the band the SNP cloud lives in)
    track = sector.add_track((60, 90))
    # subset the dataframe to this chromosome only
    chrom_num = int(name.replace("chr", ""))
    df = gwas[gwas["chrom"] == chrom_num]
    # CALL: scatter SNP position vs -log10(p) inside the track
    track.scatter(df["pos"].to_numpy(), df["nlog10p"].to_numpy(),
                  s=1.5, color=GREY, alpha=0.6)

fig = circos.plotfig(figsize=(7, 7))                    # CALL
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}

<!-- slide 52 -->
## Circos · Step 4 — Hits & Threshold Ring {.smaller}

[pyCirclize · build]{.eyebrow}

### 4 · Colour what crossed the line

The same logic as the linear Manhattan: a dashed ring at `-log10(5e-8)`, and the SNPs above it re-drawn in red on top of the grey cloud. The threshold becomes a circle; significance becomes everything that pokes through it.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="17-25"}
from pycirclize import Circos

gwas = load_gwas("height").copy()
gwas["nlog10p"] = -np.log10(gwas["pval"])
chrom_len = gwas.groupby("chrom")["pos"].max().to_dict()
sectors = {f"chr{c}": chrom_len[c] for c in sorted(chrom_len)}
gw_thresh = -np.log10(5e-8)                          # genome-wide significance

circos = Circos(sectors, space=2)                    # CREATE

for sector in circos.sectors:
    name = sector.name                                 # pyCirclize: list of Sector(name=...)
    sector.text(name, r=108, size=8, color=INK)
    sector.axis(fc=CREAM, ec=INK, lw=0.6)

    track = sector.add_track((60, 90))
    chrom_num = int(name.replace("chr", ""))
    df = gwas[gwas["chrom"] == chrom_num]
    # background cloud — grey
    track.scatter(df["pos"].to_numpy(), df["nlog10p"].to_numpy(),
                  s=1.5, color=GREY, alpha=0.6)
    # hits — significant SNPs re-drawn red, larger
    hits = df[df["pval"] < 5e-8]
    if not hits.empty:                                       # most chroms have no hits
        track.scatter(hits["pos"].to_numpy(), hits["nlog10p"].to_numpy(),
                      s=10, color=RED, alpha=0.95)
    # dashed threshold ring at y = -log10(5e-8)
    track.line([0, chrom_len[chrom_num]], [gw_thresh, gw_thresh],
               color=RED, lw=0.6, ls="--")

fig = circos.plotfig(figsize=(7, 7))                 # CALL
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}

<!-- slide 53 -->
## Circos · Step 5 — Chord Links {.smaller}

[pyCirclize · build]{.eyebrow}

### 5 · Connect the hits across chromosomes

The headline feature of any Circos plot: **chords**. `circos.link((sector_a, start, end), (sector_b, start, end))` draws a quadratic Bezier through the centre joining two intervals. We use it here to connect the top-5 most significant SNPs to each other — real publications use the same primitive for translocations, synteny blocks, or cis-/trans-regulatory pairs.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="28-37"}
from pycirclize import Circos

gwas = load_gwas("height").copy()
gwas["nlog10p"] = -np.log10(gwas["pval"])
chrom_len = gwas.groupby("chrom")["pos"].max().to_dict()
sectors = {f"chr{c}": chrom_len[c] for c in sorted(chrom_len)}
gw_thresh = -np.log10(5e-8)

circos = Circos(sectors, space=2)                              # CREATE

for sector in circos.sectors:
    name = sector.name                                 # pyCirclize: list of Sector(name=...)
    sector.text(name, r=108, size=8, color=INK)
    sector.axis(fc=CREAM, ec=INK, lw=0.6)
    track = sector.add_track((60, 90))
    chrom_num = int(name.replace("chr", ""))
    df = gwas[gwas["chrom"] == chrom_num]
    track.scatter(df["pos"].to_numpy(), df["nlog10p"].to_numpy(),
                  s=1.5, color=GREY, alpha=0.6)
    hits = df[df["pval"] < 5e-8]
    if not hits.empty:                                       # most chroms have no hits
        track.scatter(hits["pos"].to_numpy(), hits["nlog10p"].to_numpy(),
                      s=10, color=RED, alpha=0.95)
    track.line([0, chrom_len[chrom_num]], [gw_thresh, gw_thresh],
               color=RED, lw=0.6, ls="--")

# pick the top-5 strongest hits across the whole genome
top5 = gwas.nsmallest(5, "pval").reset_index(drop=True)

# draw a chord between consecutive pairs (1-2, 2-3, 3-4, 4-5)
for i in range(len(top5) - 1):
    a, b = top5.iloc[i], top5.iloc[i + 1]
    if a["chrom"] == b["chrom"]:                               # skip intra-chrom
        continue
    # link: two (sector, start, end) tuples; +-1bp gives a thin chord
    circos.link((f"chr{a['chrom']}", int(a['pos']) - 1, int(a['pos']) + 1),
                (f"chr{b['chrom']}", int(b['pos']) - 1, int(b['pos']) + 1),
                color=PURPLE, alpha=0.55)

fig = circos.plotfig(figsize=(7, 7))                           # CALL
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}

<!-- slide 54 -->
## Circos · Takeaway {.smaller}

[pyCirclize · recap]{.eyebrow}

### Three primitives, any biology

::: {.takeaway}
[The recipe]{.tl}
1. **Sectors** — `{name: length}` defines the ring; one wedge per chromosome.
2. **Tracks** — `sector.add_track((inner_r, outer_r))` is a concentric data band; stack as many as the eye can read.
3. **Links** — `circos.link(...)` is a chord between two intervals; the answer to "which moved with which".
:::

Circular plots trade per-chromosome zoom for cross-chromosome reach. Use them when the story is **relationships, not values** — translocations, synteny, Hi-C contacts, regulator-target pairs. Same logic for bacterial genomes (one sector per replicon), for metagenomes (one sector per MAG), even for protein domains (one sector per chain).
